planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring into deep, constantly moist, humus-rich soil near a pond edge or woodland stream bank.

directions: This Dutch selection carries large palmate leaves that cycle through color over the season: chocolate-brown on emergence, green by midsummer, bronzing again, then deepening to red once autumn cold arrives. Branched plumes of pale pink flowers aging to burgundy-red rise above the foliage from midsummer into early fall. Give it steady moisture and some shelter from drying wind, since the thin leaves scorch quickly if the soil ever dries out, and avoid dividing the clump more often than every several years.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, reliably moist soil sheltered from cold, drying winds.

directions: Selected by the plant-collecting Wynn-Jones family of Crûg Farm Plants in Wales, this cultivar forms a mound of bronze-tinged, deeply divided leaves beneath stout plumes of deep pink flowers that intensify toward true cardinal-red as the plumes mature into autumn, holding color far longer than most Rodgersia pinnata forms. It performs best in deep, humus-rich soil that never dries out, mulched to buffer summer heat around the root zone. Protect young spring growth from late frost and slug damage, and divide only occasionally since established clumps resent disturbance.

planting.note: Plant dormant tuberous roots or divisions in spring, 4-5 inches deep, into rich woodland soil that stays evenly moist through summer.

directions: A member of the ginger family related to true gingers, this Himalayan perennial produces strap-shaped, upright leaves and loose clusters of orchid-like purple-violet flowers marked with milky streaks and a mulberry throat. 'Vincent' is valued for blooming unusually late and long, carrying fresh flowers from midsummer right up until the first hard frost cuts the foliage down. Site it in dappled shade with rich, moisture-retentive soil, and mulch over winter in colder parts of its range since new shoots emerge late and can be damaged by hard freezes before they appear.

planting.note: Set out container plants after the last frost into well-drained, humus-rich soil in bright shade.

directions: Native to the Himalayan foothills of Nepal, this soft-textured mounding perennial carries fuzzy, drip-tipped leaves and cone-shaped purple buds that open into tubular blue-violet flowers packed into dense terminal spikes. Bloom begins in late summer and continues strong right up until frost, a season when few other shade perennials are still flowering. It tolerates lean soil under trees and shrubs but performs best with good drainage and consistent moisture in bright, dappled shade; where winters dip below its comfort zone, mulch heavily or treat it as a late-planted seasonal perennial.

planting.note: Divide and transplant in early spring or immediately after flowering into humus-rich soil that stays damp through the growing season.

directions: This selection of mourning widow cranesbill carries nodding, five-petaled flowers in a soft pale lilac-blue, a notably lighter shade than the near-black blooms typical of the species, set against mid-green foliage marked with dark blotches near the leaf center. It flowers from late spring into early summer and self-sows modestly in damp woodland conditions without becoming a nuisance. Grow it in part shade with consistently moist soil for the richest foliage, and divide congested clumps every few years to keep it vigorous.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring into constantly moist, rich soil; thrives at pond margins and in low, boggy spots.

directions: A compact leopard plant whose rounded, glossy leaves emerge dark burgundy before settling toward olive green by midsummer, with purple undersides that show whenever the foliage lifts in a breeze. Clusters of yellow-orange daisy flowers rise on dark garnet stems in summer, giving strong contrast against the foliage. Because the broad leaves wilt readily in heat, keep the soil reliably moist and give afternoon shade, especially in warmer zones; its smaller stature compared to other Ligularia dentata selections makes it a better fit for tighter shade-garden spaces.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into evenly moist, humus-rich soil in deep or dappled shade.

directions: Known under this older Japanese trade name, this toad lily sends up medium-green foliage topped from late summer into fall with white, purple-spotted flowers whose tepals flush amethyst toward the tips. It is one of the earlier toad lilies to begin flowering, extending bloom color in the shade garden before most other Tricyrtis selections open. Keep the soil from ever drying out and mulch with leaf litter to mimic its native woodland floor conditions, dividing congested clumps every few years in early spring to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into medium to wet, humusy, slightly acidic soil that never fully dries.

directions: Upright, arching stems carry broad, glossy medium-green leaves and pure white, lily-shaped flowers tipped with lavender-pink anthers, opening earlier in the season than most toad lily cultivars so color starts in midsummer rather than waiting for fall. The plant spreads gently by stolons, slowly knitting into a loose colony without becoming aggressive. Grow it in part to full shade with constantly moist, organically rich soil, and leave the spent stems standing into winter if seed heads or late pollinator visits are wanted before a spring cleanup.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring into rich, consistently moist soil in part shade.

directions: This wild species toad lily, native across a wide swath of eastern Asia into Taiwan, forms a tight clump of upright, ladder-like stems clothed in glossy, purple-speckled leaves. From midsummer into early fall it carries large, branched sprays of white, orchid-shaped flowers whose tips flush amethyst and blue, a larger and taller presence than most garden hybrid toad lilies. It is the wild parent behind several popular cultivars and performs best in semi-shaded, slightly moist, rich soil; in its cooler hardiness range, mulch the crown well for winter protection.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into well-drained soil; established clumps tolerate dry shade though growth is slower there.

directions: Collected by plantsman Roy Lancaster on Wudang Mountain in Hubei, China, this selection of Chinese fairy wing makes a tighter, smaller clump than typical Epimedium stellulatum, with glossy, spiny-edged evergreen leaves that emerge bronzy-pink before turning green for summer. Loose spikes of small, star-shaped white flowers with prominent yellow stamens appear in spring, just as the new leaf color is at its best. Once established it is notably drought tolerant and deer resistant, making it a reliable groundcover choice for dry shade under trees where moisture-hungry shade perennials struggle.
